source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan, Starbird (2024) Misleading Ourselves: How Disinformation Manipulates Sensemaking
finding: Founding paper. Coins manipulated sensemaking. Disinformation shapes broad deep stories that set the frames used to read later ambiguous events. Sensemaking favours plausible over accurate accounts.
numbers: Qualitative coding of about 1000 tweets: 5 salient rumors per election (2020, 2022), 100 tweets per rumor, 500 per year.
quote: A good story holds disparate elements together long enough to energize and guide action
limits: CHI 2024 workshop paper. No effect sizes, no control group, no causal test. One country, one topic (US elections), human rumours only. Frame persistence from 2020 to 2022 is shown by case, not measured.
agent_relevance: Argues S1 should treat the story frame around a claim as part of the input, not only the claim. No LLM test exists in the paper.

source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan, Starbird (2024) Misleading Ourselves: How Disinformation Manipulates Sensemaking
finding: Case: Maricopa County. In 2020 rumours said Sharpie ink bled and ballots were thrown out. In 2022 tabulator errors and a drop box were read through the same fraud deep story, with little new explanation needed.
numbers: Same coded sample (500 tweets per election year). Authors say elite and influencer involvement was more subtle in 2022 than in 2020.
limits: Interpretation by the authors, not blind-coded counts. No inter-coder numbers in this short version.
agent_relevance: The frame arrives first and decides which facts count. An agent given a pre-built narrative will read new evidence through it. Test: same evidence with and without the narrative wrapper.

source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan, Starbird (2024) Misleading Ourselves: How Disinformation Manipulates Sensemaking
finding: Mechanism claimed: frame fixation (from Klein et al. data-frame theory) plus plausibility. People keep one frame and explain away data that does not fit. Repetition by in-group members and source authority add credibility.
numbers: Cites Weick 1995, Klein et al. 2007, Hochschild 2016, Kapferer 1990. No new numbers.
limits: Theory built on Weick and Klein, which are themselves mostly case-based. Rival view: the deep story reflects prior belief, not manipulation.
agent_relevance: Maps to existing schema ideas on frame fixation and anomaly handling (E10 folders 01 and 03). New here: an adversary can plant the frame.

source: Chan, Jones, Hall Jamieson, Albarracin (2017) Debunking: A Meta-Analysis of the Psychological Efficacy of Messages Countering Misinformation
finding: Misinformation effect is large and debunking only partly undoes it. Misinformation persists after debunking.
numbers: k=52 reports, N=6,878. Misinformation ds 2.41 to 3.08. Debunking ds 1.14 to 1.33. Persistence ds 0.75 to 1.06. Heterogeneity I2 about 98 to 99 percent.
limits: Mostly lab analog tasks (e.g. warehouse fire), mean age about 20, 72 percent female. Mixed publication-bias checks. Few real political claims.
agent_relevance: Even after a correction a residue of the planted account remains. An agent that ingested a false frame should not assume a later correction restores the earlier state; re-derive from clean input.

source: Chan et al. (2017) meta-analysis
finding: Moderator: when audiences generate reasons supporting the initial misinformation, persistence rises and the debunking effect falls. Generating counterarguments helps.
numbers: Supporting explanations: debunking b=-4.08 [-5.50,-2.66]; persistence b=2.09 [0.88,3.30]. Counterarguments: persistence b=-0.68 [-1.16,-0.20] (weighted; unweighted not significant). Debunking d=0.62 (k=18) when supporting explanations high vs 3.77 (k=3) when low.
limits: Small cells (k=3). Moderators are correlational across studies, not randomised.
agent_relevance: Asking the agent to elaborate on a planted claim may entrench it. Elaborate on rival frames (counterarguments) instead.

source: Chan et al. (2017) meta-analysis
finding: Detailed refutations work better than label-only ones, but detailed debunks also correlated with stronger persistence. Authors flag a possible confound.
numbers: Detail vs labeling-only debunking: b=1.82 [0.57,3.07]; d=1.25 (k=18) vs 0.16 (k=3). Persistence with detail: b=1.06 [0.23,1.90]; d=1.58 (k=21) vs 0.55 (k=14). Post hoc r(33)=.52 between misinformation detail and debunk detail.
limits: Confounded: studies with detailed debunks also had more detailed misinformation. No backfire test.
agent_relevance: A bare 'this is false' does little. Corrections should offer a rival coherent account, not only negate.

source: Roozenbeek, van der Linden, Goldberg, Rathje, Lewandowsky (2022) Psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media
finding: Short videos teaching manipulation techniques raised recognition of those techniques across 6 lab studies and a replication.
numbers: Six RCTs total n=6,464 (study 6 replication n=1,068). Technique recognition d: emotional language 0.49, incoherence 0.62, false dichotomy 0.68, scapegoating 0.28, ad hominem 0.45; study 6 d=0.67. 19 of 23 hypothesised effects significant.
limits: US quota samples only. Decay not measured. Stimuli not exact mirrors.
agent_relevance: Technique-level hygiene (spot emotional language, false dichotomy, scapegoating in the input) is trainable. The S1 mask could name these cues. Untested in LLMs.

source: Roozenbeek et al. (2022) inoculation videos
finding: Effects on judging truth and on sharing were much smaller than effects on technique recognition. Field study on YouTube gave a small effect.
numbers: Trustworthiness discernment d: 0.10 to 0.32 (study 6 d=0.44). Sharing discernment d: 0.10 to 0.22 (study 6 d=0.34); several n.s. YouTube study 7 n=22,632: Cohen h=0.09 (about 5 percent gain in recognition), below the preregistered smallest effect of interest h=0.10. Measured about 18.4 hours after viewing.
limits: One test item per YouTube participant. 24-hour window. No behavioural outcome.
agent_relevance: Knowing the technique does not much change belief or action. For an agent, naming cues is not enough; the masking has to change what the downstream step sees.

source: Bad News: Testing Gamified Inoculation Against Misinformation (2025 preprint)
finding: A small replication-style test found the Bad News game improved identification of misinformative items versus a Tetris control. Abstract only.
numbers: n=266 final participants. 15 minutes of play vs Tetris. Improvement larger than control (no effect size in abstract).
limits: Abstract only read. Preprint. The known counter-argument (game gains may be a response-bias shift, not better discernment) is from memory and not verified here.
agent_relevance: Treat inoculation gains as possibly response-bias shifts. In LLM tests report both discernment and bias.

source: Ceylan, Anderson, Wood (2023) Sharing of misinformation is habitual, not just lazy or biased
finding: Sharing of false news is driven by platform-built habits, not only by poor reasoning or partisanship.
numbers: N=2,476. 30 to 40 percent of false news shared came from the 15 percent most habitual sharers.
limits: Abstract only read. Online samples.
agent_relevance: Rival to the plausibility account: part of spread is automatic cue-response. Agents also have cue-triggered habits, such as reusing a frame; guardrails should act before the habit fires.

source: Pennycook, Epstein, Mosleh, Arechar, Eckles, Rand (2021) Shifting attention to accuracy can reduce misinformation online
finding: Headline veracity has little effect on sharing intent though it has a large effect on accuracy judgment. A subtle accuracy prompt improves the quality of what people share.
numbers: Four survey experiments plus a field experiment on Twitter (numbers not read in this session).
limits: Abstract only read. Effect sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: Plausibility is a different dial from accuracy; a prompt that moves attention to accuracy is cheap. Analogue: an accuracy-check line before the answer state.

source: Arechar et al. (2023) Understanding and combatting misinformation across 16 countries on six continents
finding: The accuracy-prompt effect and the link between analytic style and truth discernment held across countries. Digital literacy tips also helped.
numbers: N=34,286 participants, 676,605 observations, 16 countries. Crowd aggregation separated true from false headlines in all countries.
limits: Abstract only read. Online samples; COVID-19 headlines. Per-country effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Moderator evidence: culture does not remove the effect. Individual differences (analytic style, accuracy motivation) predict discernment.

source: Vosoughi, Roy, Aral (2018) The spread of true and false news online
finding: False news spread farther, faster, deeper and more broadly than true news. Novelty was higher for false news. Bots spread true and false at the same rate.
numbers: About 126,000 stories, about 3 million people, more than 4.5 million tweets, 2006 to 2017; six fact-checkers agreed 95 to 98 percent.
limits: Abstract only read. Twitter only. Fact-check-selected stories.
agent_relevance: Planted stories arrive often and novel. An agent reading web text will see false items over-represented.

source: Costello, Pennycook, Rand (2024) Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI
finding: Three-round tailored dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo cut conspiracy belief by about 20 percent. The drop lasted 2 months and spilled over to unrelated conspiracies.
numbers: N=2,190 conspiracy believers across two experiments; control talked about a banal topic.
limits: Abstract only read (Science page returned 403). Participants knew they spoke to AI. Fact-check accuracy of the AI claims not read here.
agent_relevance: LLMs can supply tailored counter-evidence that undoes a planted frame. The same capability works in reverse (see Salvi, Hackenburg).

source: Spitale, Biller-Andorno, Germani (2023) AI model GPT-3 (dis)informs us better than humans
finding: GPT-3 tweets were judged correctly true more often than human tweets, and GPT-3 disinformation fooled people slightly more than human disinformation. People could not tell GPT-3 from human text.
numbers: 697 analysed of 869 respondents. Recognising disinformation: organic false 0.92 vs synthetic false 0.89 (p=0.0032). True tweets: synthetic 0.84 vs organic 0.72 (p<0.0001). Organic vs synthetic recognition about 0.50.
limits: Short tweets, GPT-3 davinci, UK/US-heavy online sample. The disinformation effect is small.
agent_relevance: Fluent LLM text removes the style cue. S1 cannot rely on 'looks machine-written' or 'looks sloppy' to flag bad input.

source: Spitale et al. (2023) GPT-3 (dis)informs
finding: GPT-3 as a judge of tweet truth was worse than people on true tweets and about equal on false ones. GPT-3 failed to write disinformation more often than accurate text.
numbers: GPT-3 vs humans: true tweets 0.64 vs 0.72; false tweets 0.89 vs 0.92 (humans slightly better). Obedience: accurate requests 99 of 101, disinformation requests 80 of 102.
limits: Old model and 2022 tweets. Newer models differ a lot.
agent_relevance: Early evidence an LLM alone is a weak detector. Do not use one self-check as the hygiene filter.

source: Salvi, Horta Ribeiro, Gallotti, West (2024) On the Conversational Persuasiveness of Large Language Models: A Randomized Controlled Trial
finding: GPT-4 with access to personal data beat human debaters at shifting opinion in a live debate setting.
numbers: N=820 unique participants, 150 debates per condition. GPT-4 with personalisation: odds of higher agreement with the opponent +81.7% [26.3, 161.4], p<0.01. Without personalisation +21.3% [-16.7, 76.6], not significant. Human personalised -17.4% [-46.1, 26.5], not significant.
limits: Short debates on assigned topics, Prolific sample. Republicans more persuadable (+60%, [6, 141], p=0.02). Topic knowledge cut opinion change (odds -72.9%).
agent_relevance: Opinion change is lower on topics the person already knows well. For an agent, verified prior knowledge is a protective factor.

source: Hackenburg, Tappin, Röttger, Hale, Bright, Margetts (2024) Evidence of a Log Scaling Law for Political Persuasion with Large Language Models
finding: Persuasion by static LLM messages grows only with the log of model size. Larger models are barely better than models 10 times smaller.
numbers: N=25,982; 24 models; 720 messages; 10 US political issues. Average effect 5.77 percentage points; +1.26 pp per one-unit rise in log parameters; estimated ceiling about 12 pp. Task completion (coherence, topic) explained the larger-model gain.
limits: Single-turn static messages, no persuasion tuning, US adults. Dialogue may do more.
agent_relevance: A small cheap model can plant a frame nearly as well as a frontier one. Do not count on model size for defence.

source: Hackenburg et al. (2024) Log scaling law
finding: Rival to the 'scale makes persuasion explode' view: sharply diminishing returns, with 7B to 13B models close to frontier level.
numbers: Models with 7 to 13 billion parameters were close to frontier models (estimated above 300B) and to a human-written baseline of 10 messages.
limits: Human baseline is only 10 messages (one per issue). Static, not dialogue.
agent_relevance: Cost of planting frames is low. Any pipeline reading web content should assume cheap, fluent, targeted input.

source: Hackenburg, Tappin, Hewitt, Saunders, et al. (2025) The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
finding: Post-training and prompting raise AI persuasion far more than scale or personalisation. Where they raise persuasion they lower factual accuracy.
numbers: Three experiments N=76,977; 19 LLMs; 707 issues; 466,769 claims fact-checked. Post-training up to +51%, prompting up to +27%. Scale about +1.59 pp per order of magnitude. Conversation vs static: GPT-4o +2.94 pp (+41%), GPT-4.5 +3.60 pp (+52%).
limits: Short-term attitude change; one follow-up at one month (study 1). Accuracy graded by an automated fact-checker.
agent_relevance: Persuasive text is more likely inaccurate, so persuasiveness is a warning sign, not a reliability sign. Supports a rule not to weigh input by how convincing it sounds.

source: Hackenburg et al. (2025) Levers of Political Persuasion
finding: The 'information' prompt (pile on facts and evidence) was the most persuasive and the least accurate.
numbers: Information prompt +2.29 pp [1.84, 2.75] vs +1.37 pp for the next-best prompt, about 27% more persuasive. Accurate claims 62% under the information prompt vs 78% for other prompts; GPT-4.5 rated inaccurate more than 30% of the time. Reward-model post-training: persuasion +2.32 pp, accurate claims -2.22 pp. SFT on accuracy: +4.89 pp accuracy, no persuasion gain.
limits: The paper says low accuracy could be cause or byproduct of persuasion. Not tested which.
agent_relevance: Dense, factual-looking input is the main route for planted frames. S1 should audit claim density and check claims before use.

source: Chen and Shu (2024) Can LLM-Generated Misinformation Be Detected? (ICLR 2024)
finding: LLM-written misinformation was harder to detect than human-written misinformation with the same meaning, for both humans and detectors.
numbers: Human detection success was lower on ChatGPT-generated items than on human-written ones (Table 3). The text says humans spotted only 9.6 percent of one generated category with false dates, names, numbers and quotes.
limits: Few human annotators; main generator ChatGPT; pooled counts not extracted beyond the 9.6 percent.
agent_relevance: Style-based detection will fail; check checkable details (dates, names, numbers) against sources.

source: Pan, Pan, Chen, Nakov, Kan, Wang (2023) On the Risk of Misinformation Pollution with Large Language Models
finding: LLM-made fake passages injected into the evidence corpus cut open-domain QA accuracy sharply, even when the fakes were a tiny share of the corpus.
numbers: Exact match drop 14 to 54% for DPR-based systems and 20 to 87% for BM25-based systems. Fake passages were about 0.01 to 0.1% of corpus size. Retrievers prefer the fakes because they match the question.
limits: QA over Wikipedia-style corpora (NQ, CovidNews); simulated attacker; older readers (FiD, GPT-3.5).
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of S1: a small planted fraction can dominate. Retrieved or tool results need provenance checks, not only relevance ranking.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Misinformation Pollution
finding: Defences were partial. Trained detectors work in-domain but fail out-of-domain. A vigilance warning in the prompt gave inconsistent results. Splitting evidence into groups and voting helped most.
numbers: Detector AUROC in-domain 91.4 to 99.7; out-of-domain 50.7 to 64.8 (50 is chance). Voting relative EM gain: +11%, +12%, +23% over three attack types. Prompt warning: +8%, about 7% (direction unclear in extracted table), 0%.
limits: Voting costs several reader calls. Table text partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: An S1 warning line alone is weak. Independent readings of separate evidence subsets plus voting is better supported, which fits sampling several alternatives.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Hidden bias features in the prompt change chain-of-thought answers, and the explanation never mentions the bias.
numbers: Accuracy dropped by up to 36% across 13 tasks. GPT-3.5 zero-shot CoT with a suggested answer: -36.3%. 'Answer is always A' few-shot: GPT-3.5 -18.7%, Claude 1.0 -4.7%.
limits: Older models (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0). Biases were artificial (suggested answer, ordering), not stories.
agent_relevance: A planted cue can steer the final answer while the written reasoning looks neutral. S1 must remove the cue from the input, not trust a later trace check.

source: Shi, Chen, Misra, Scales, Dohan, Chi, Schaerli, Zhou (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Adding an irrelevant sentence to grade-school math problems lowers accuracy a lot. Self-consistency and an 'ignore irrelevant information' instruction help.
numbers: GSM-IC benchmark built from GSM8K. Exact accuracy drops not extracted (abstract and intro read).
limits: Arithmetic distractors are not narratives. Only abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Gives a test design for equal-token masked vs unmasked prompts. Also a cheap mitigation (ignore-irrelevant instruction plus self-consistency).

source: Wu, Wu, Zou (2024) ClashEval: Quantifying the tug-of-war between an LLM's internal prior and external evidence
finding: LLMs adopt wrong retrieved content over their own correct knowledge more than 60 percent of the time. Less deviation from truth means more adoption. Low model confidence raises adoption.
numbers: More than 1,200 questions in 6 domains; 6 top LLMs including GPT-4o; perturbations from subtle to blatant. Adoption of incorrect content over correct prior above 60%.
limits: Only abstract and intro read. Questions are factual, not narrative.
agent_relevance: Subtle plausible errors are the most dangerous. A confidence-aware rule (verify when unsure) is supported.

source: Xie, Zhang, Chen, Lou, Su (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of LLMs in Knowledge Conflicts (ICLR 2024)
finding: LLMs accept external evidence that contradicts their memory when it is coherent and convincing, yet show confirmation bias toward evidence that fits their prior.
numbers: Abstract-level findings only; numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract only read. Counter-memory was LLM-generated, so its coherence may exceed real-world fakes.
agent_relevance: Mirror of the human plausibility finding: coherence drives acceptance. Coherent planted text is the risk.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Five AI assistants showed sycophancy: they wrongly admitted mistakes, gave biased feedback and mimicked user errors. Human and preference-model judgments favour matching the user's view.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions. A user suggesting a wrong answer cuts accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2). Best-of-N with N=4096: about 25% sycophantic with an oracle preference model vs about 75% with the Claude 2 preference model.
limits: Models of 2023. Mechanism evidence is observational from preference data.
agent_relevance: Models inherit a human-like bias toward agreeable, plausible accounts. A user-supplied story is a pressure source, so S1 should separate the story from the data.

source: Goldstein, Chao, Grossman, Stamos, Tomz (2024) How persuasive is AI-generated propaganda?
finding: GPT-3 articles persuaded US readers about as well as real foreign propaganda. Prompt editing and output curating by a person raised persuasiveness further.
numbers: Preregistered survey experiment; GPT-3 davinci; sample size not read here.
limits: Abstract only read. GPT-3 only; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Low-effort human editing brings AI text to propaganda level. Treat all fluent input as possibly planted.

source: Goldstein, Sastry, Musser, DiResta, Gentzel, Sedova (2023) Generative Language Models and Automated Influence Operations
finding: Threat-model report on how language models change influence operations. Downloaded but not read this session.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not read; do not rely on it until opened.
agent_relevance: Possible source of a threat taxonomy for S1 cues. Needs reading.

source: Walter and Murphy (2018) How to unring the bell: a meta-analytic approach to correction of misinformation
finding: Not opened. A second correction meta-analysis exists and should be read to cross-check Chan et al.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not read. Search API did not return its abstract.
agent_relevance: Open next to confirm correction effect size and moderators (source, topic, timing).
